overseas-buyer-inquiries.title: How Chinese Manufacturers Can Win Overseas Buyer Inquiries | Hurfi
overseas-buyer-inquiries.h1: How Chinese manufacturers can win more overseas buyer inquiries
overseas-buyer-inquiries.description: A guide for Chinese factories: why marketplaces are not enough, what overseas buyers check, and how a website, search and LinkedIn work together to produce inquiries.
overseas-buyer-inquiries.lead: Marketplaces and trade shows still matter. But many overseas buyers now start with a search, a LinkedIn profile or a recommendation — and then check the factory’s own website before they write. This guide explains how to be ready for that check.

sections.h2: Why a marketplace listing is not enough on its own
p: B2B marketplaces are useful: they bring traffic and a familiar way to request quotes. The problem is that every supplier on the platform looks similar. Your listing sits next to dozens of others, often with the same photos, the same claims and prices that invite a race to the bottom.

A buyer who is serious about a long-term supplier usually wants to know more than a listing can show: who you are, what you make yourself, what you outsource, which standards you work to and who they will deal with after the first order. That information belongs on a website you control.

sections.h2: What an overseas buyer checks before writing to you
p: Before an engineer or purchasing manager sends a first message, they are trying to answer a few simple questions:
ul: Is this a real manufacturer, and where is the factory?
Do they make the product I need, to the specification and standard I need?
Can they handle my volumes, and what is the minimum order?
Who will answer me, in which language, and how quickly?
What happens after I send an inquiry?
p2: If your website answers these questions in plain English, the buyer arrives at the first conversation already half-convinced. If it does not, many buyers simply move on without telling you why.

sections.h2: Build the website around those questions
p: A factory website that produces inquiries is usually less about design and more about structure:
ul: Product or capability pages with specifications in HTML, not only in a PDF.
A factory and quality page with real photos, equipment, certificates and their scope.
Application or industry pages that speak to the buyer’s problem.
A clear inquiry path: what to send (drawings, quantities, target date) and what you will send back.
p2: We go through the practical checklist in [what a manufacturer website needs for RFQs](/insights/manufacturer-website-rfq-checklist/).

sections.h2: Let search bring the right buyers
p: Google search works best for manufacturers when it targets the specific questions buyers ask at the specification stage — product types, materials, standards, tolerances, compatibility — rather than broad phrases such as “China manufacturer”, which mostly attract price shoppers.

This is slower than buying ads, and nobody can honestly promise a ranking. But pages that answer real technical questions keep working for years, and the buyers who arrive through them tend to be better qualified. Our [SEO service](/services/seo/) is built around this approach.

sections.h2: Use LinkedIn to show the people and the process
p: Buyers want to know who they will deal with. A company page with no posts, or posts made only of stock images, does not help. Short posts that show real production steps, inspection, packing and the engineers behind the product are more convincing — as long as you only share what your customers allow you to share.

LinkedIn is also where many buyers will check the person who replies to their inquiry. Make sure that person’s profile is complete and consistent with the website. See [social media management](/services/social-media-management/) for how we approach this.

All of this is wasted if an inquiry waits three days for a reply, or if the reply ignores the buyer’s question. Decide who answers inquiries, in which language, and within what time. Use the same company name, address and contact details on the website, LinkedIn and every marketplace profile, so a buyer who checks finds one consistent picture.

Track qualified inquiries, not only traffic. Connect Google Search Console and a privacy-respecting analytics tool, note where each inquiry came from, and review it monthly. That tells you which pages and channels are worth more effort — and which are not.

faq: Should we stop using B2B marketplaces?
Not necessarily. Many factories use both. Your own website gives buyers a place to verify you and gives you inquiries that do not depend on one platform.
How long does it take for search to bring inquiries?
It depends on your market, competition and the state of your current site. Nobody can honestly promise a timeline; regular reporting shows whether it is working.

factory-website-trust-signals.title: Factory Website Trust Signals Overseas Buyers Look For | Hurfi
factory-website-trust-signals.h1: Why overseas buyers hesitate on factory websites — and what to fix
factory-website-trust-signals.description: The trust signals overseas buyers look for on a Chinese factory website, the mistakes that make a real factory look unreliable, and how to fix them.
factory-website-trust-signals.lead: Overseas buyers have learned to be careful. Many have met trading companies presented as factories, copied photos and certificates that did not check out. A real factory can lose an inquiry simply because its website looks like those. Here is what buyers look for, written from the factory’s side.

p: The first signal is a clear, consistent identity:
ul: Your registered company name in English, the same on every page, profile and document.
A real factory address, ideally with a map, and photos that match it.
Named people a buyer can contact, with roles — not only a generic form.
The year the company was founded and what you actually manufacture in-house.
p2: If you are a trading company or work with partner factories, say so plainly. Buyers accept that much more easily than discovering it later.

sections.h2: Show the factory, not stock images
p: Stock photos of generic factories are recognised immediately. A few honest photos and short videos of your own production lines, inspection area and warehouse are worth more than a polished render. Name the equipment where it matters to the buyer — for example the machine types or test instruments you use.
Certificates are only useful if a buyer can verify them. For each one, show:
ul: The certificate itself, readable, not just a logo.
The certificate holder name, which should match your company name.
The scope — which products or sites it covers.
The issuing body and the validity date.
p2: Do not show logos for certifications you do not hold, or imply that one model’s approval covers a whole range. Experienced buyers check, and a single mismatch can end the conversation.

sections.h2: Put the technical detail on the page
p: Specifications hidden in a downloadable catalog, or published as images, make a site feel thin. Put the key data in HTML tables on each product or capability page, with units and test conditions. This helps buyers compare you, and it helps search engines understand what you make.
Some details make a real factory look unreliable. Check your site for:
ul: Broken links, empty pages or “coming soon” sections.
Machine-translated text and inconsistent product names.
Claims with no evidence: “No.1 in China”, “world-leading”, unexplained star ratings.
Contact details that differ between the website, LinkedIn and marketplace profiles.
A free email address as the only contact, instead of an address on your own domain.

sections.h2: Explain what happens after an inquiry
p: A buyer is more likely to write if they know what comes next: who replies, within what time, whether you sign an NDA for drawings, how samples work and what information you need for a quotation. One short paragraph near the inquiry form removes much of the hesitation.

Out-of-date certificates, old product lines and copyright years from several years ago suggest a company that is not paying attention. Set a simple review cycle — for example every quarter — to check certificates, contact details and key product pages.

faq: Do we need to show client names?
No. Many factories cannot. Capability, process, equipment and quality evidence can build trust without naming clients.
Are reviews and ratings important?
Only if they are real and verifiable. An unexplained rating is a warning sign, not a trust signal.

Yes. A [website review](/book-consultation/#book-form) covers these points. See also [website development](/services/website-development/).

manufacturer-website-rfq-checklist.title: Manufacturer Website RFQ Checklist: Pages That Get Quotes | Hurfi
manufacturer-website-rfq-checklist.h1: What a manufacturer website needs before buyers send an RFQ
manufacturer-website-rfq-checklist.description: A practical checklist of the pages, specifications and inquiry details a Chinese manufacturer website needs so overseas buyers can send a complete RFQ.
manufacturer-website-rfq-checklist.lead: A request for quotation is a buyer telling you they are ready to compare prices. Your website can make that easy — or it can make the buyer give up halfway. This checklist covers the pages and details that help an overseas buyer send a complete RFQ.

sections.h2: 1. Product or capability pages a buyer can compare
p: Every main product family or manufacturing capability should have its own page with:
ul: A clear name in the terms buyers use, not only your internal model codes.
A specification table in HTML, with units and tolerances.
Materials, finishes and options.
Downloadable datasheets, drawings or CAD files where relevant.
A request-a-quote link on the page itself.

p: Buyers want to know they are dealing with the manufacturer. Show production equipment, inspection and testing, the quality system and certificates with their scope and validity. Real photos matter more than design.
Many RFQs stall on simple questions. Answer them on the site:
ul: Minimum order quantity, or how MOQ is decided.
Typical lead time for samples and for production.
Sample policy and cost.
Incoterms you usually quote and the ports you ship from.
Payment terms you normally accept.

sections.h2: 4. An inquiry form that asks for the right things
p: A good RFQ form is short but specific. Useful fields include:
ul: Product or part, and quantity.
Target date.
Drawing or file upload, with an NDA option if you offer one.
Application or end use.
Contact details and the preferred way to reply — email, WeChat or WhatsApp.
p2: After submission, show a confirmation that says who will reply and when, and send an automatic acknowledgment. Then make sure someone actually replies.

p: Engineers often search by problem or application, not by product name. Pages that explain how your product is used in a specific industry — with the relevant standards and examples you are allowed to share — bring better-qualified visitors and give them confidence you understand their field. Our [industry pages](/industries/) show the sectors we work with.
None of this helps if search engines cannot read it:
ul: Each page has a unique, descriptive title and one clear heading.
Specifications are text, not images.
Pages load quickly on mobile, with compressed images.
The site has a sitemap, and important pages are linked from the navigation.
Google Search Console is connected so you can see how buyers find you.
p2: Our [SEO service](/services/seo/) covers this technical layer.

p: Use one company name, one set of contact details and one inquiry process across the website, LinkedIn and marketplaces. Route different requests — quotes, support, partnerships — to the right person, so none of them waits.

faq: Do we need prices on the website?
Not usually for custom or industrial products. But clear MOQ, lead-time and sample information helps buyers decide to send an RFQ.
Should the RFQ form allow file uploads?
For drawing-based work, yes. State what file types you accept and how you protect them.
Can Hurfi build this for us?
Yes — see [website development](/services/website-development/) or [book a consultation](/book-consultation/#book-form).

international-seo-checklist-for-exporter.title: International SEO Checklist for Chinese Exporters | Hurfi
international-seo-checklist-for-exporter.h1: An international SEO checklist for Chinese exporters
international-seo-checklist-for-exporter.description: A practical international SEO checklist for Chinese manufacturers: URL structure, languages, hreflang, content, technical checks and measurement.
international-seo-checklist-for-exporter.lead: Selling abroad means being found in Google by buyers who search in their own language and their own words. This checklist covers the decisions that matter most for a Chinese manufacturer’s export website, in the order we usually work through them.

p: International SEO starts with a business decision, not a technical one. List the countries where you already have certification, logistics and someone who can answer buyers. Those are your first markets.

For each one, note the language buyers search in and the words they use for your product. A German engineer and an American buyer may describe the same part differently, and both differ from the term used in your Chinese catalogue.
ul: Markets where your products are certified or can be certified soon
Markets where you can ship and support customers
Markets where you have sales staff who can reply in the buyer’s language

sections.h2: 2. Choose a URL structure you can maintain
p: Google’s guide to [managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) compares the main options: country-code domains (example.de), subdomains (de.example.com) and subdirectories (example.com/de/). Each has trade-offs in cost, maintenance and how strongly it signals a country.

For most manufacturers, one .com domain with language subdirectories is the simplest to run. It keeps all links and authority on one domain and is easy to host outside mainland China, which helps page speed for buyers abroad.
ul: Use one domain unless you have a strong reason for country domains
Keep the same structure in every language (/en/products/…, /de/products/…)
Do not rely on automatic redirects by IP address; let buyers choose the language

p: Machine translation of a Chinese catalogue rarely works. Terms get mistranslated, specifications lose their units and the pages miss the words buyers actually search for. Write the English version first, for overseas buyers, and translate from that.
Each language version should answer the same questions: what you make, to which specification and standard, how you prove quality, and how to send an RFQ.
ul: Use the buyer’s units and standard names
Translate the RFQ form and confirmation messages too
Have a native speaker or a technical reviewer check key pages

p: Hreflang annotations tell Google which page is the equivalent in another language or region. Google’s documentation on [localized versions](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) sets two rules that are often missed: each language version must list itself as well as the others, and if two pages do not point to each other, the annotations are ignored.
Use an x-default entry for the page buyers should see when no language matches.

ul: Pages load fast from your target markets — measure from outside China
Every product page has a unique, descriptive title and description
Specifications are in HTML text, not only images or PDFs
An XML sitemap lists every page you want indexed
Old URLs redirect to their new equivalents when you restructure
The RFQ form works and sends to a monitored mailbox

p: Set up [Search Console](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/search-console-start) in your company’s own account. It shows impressions, clicks and the queries that brought them, and you can filter by country and page.
Track RFQs by language and market in your analytics. Rankings are a means; qualified inquiries from the markets you chose are the goal.

Most hreflang problems on exporter sites are small and mechanical. Google’s guidelines say each language version must list itself as well as all other language versions, and that alternate URLs must be fully qualified, including https. A Spanish page that points to the English page, but not back to itself, breaks the set.
Google also describes an x-default value for pages that serve no specific language, such as a language selector or a home page that redirects. Use it when you have such a page; do not invent one.
ul: Every language version lists itself and every other version, with full https URLs.
The language codes are valid (for example en, es, de, pt-BR), not country names.
Canonical tags point to the same-language page, not to the English page.
New language pages are added to the set on all existing versions, not just one.

sections.h2: 8. Do not redirect buyers by IP address
p: It is tempting to send visitors from Germany to the German site automatically. Google’s advice on multi-regional sites is not to use IP analysis to adapt content, because location detection is unreliable and Google may not be able to crawl all variations of the site. Instead, give each version its own URL and add a visible language or region selector.
This also helps buyers. A purchasing manager in Dubai may prefer English; an engineer in Switzerland may want German or French. Let them choose, and remember their choice.

sections.h2: 9. Plan content per market, not just translation
p: Translation alone rarely wins rankings in a new market. Buyers search with local terms, standards and units. A pump that is sold by flow rate in m³/h in Europe may be searched by GPM in the United States. A cable may need UL references for North America and CE or IEC references for Europe.

Before you translate, list the ten product pages that matter most in each market, and check which terms, units and certifications buyers there use. Then write — or adapt — those pages first. Smaller, better pages in a market beat a full but weak copy of the English site.
ul: Local units and standards on every specification table.
Market-specific certifications and documents linked from the product page.
Contact options that suit the market: business hours, languages and response times.

faq: What is international SEO?

It is the work of making a website findable in search engines in more than one country or language: choosing a URL structure, writing each language version, connecting them with hreflang and measuring results by market.
Do we need a separate website for every country?
Usually not. Google documents several options; for most manufacturers, one domain with language subdirectories is the easiest to maintain.
Is machine translation good enough?
Rarely for product pages. It often gets technical terms and units wrong and misses the words buyers search for. Translate from a well-written English version and have key pages reviewed.
What happens if hreflang is wrong?
Google may ignore it. Each version must list itself and the others, and the links must go both ways.
Should we redirect visitors by IP address?
It is better to let visitors choose. Automatic redirects can stop buyers and search engines from reaching the version they need.
Does hosting in China hurt international SEO?
It can make pages slow for buyers abroad. Many exporters host the export site outside mainland China for speed.
Which language should we start with?
English, for most exporters, because it covers many markets. Add other languages where you have buyers and staff who can reply.
How do we know it is working?
Search Console shows impressions and clicks by country and page; analytics shows inquiries by market. Look at both.
Can Hurfi do this for us?
Yes. Our SEO and website development services cover structure, content, hreflang and measurement for exporters.
svc: Language-ready site structure, translated RFQ forms and fast hosting for buyers abroad.
Market selection, keyword research per language, hreflang and Search Console reporting by country.
Campaigns per country and language once the pages exist, measured by RFQs.
LinkedIn content in English that supports the markets you chose.
extra_claims: Google compares ccTLDs, subdomains and subdirectories for multi-regional sites.
Each language version must list itself; if two pages do not point to each other the tags are ignored.
Search Console shows impressions, clicks and queries.
Each language version must list itself and all other language versions; alternate URLs must be fully qualified including https.
x-default value for pages with no specific language, such as language selectors or auto-redirecting home pages.
Do not use IP analysis to adapt content; location detection is unreliable and Google may not crawl all variations.

choosing-an-export-marketing-agency.title: How to Choose an Export Marketing Agency | Hurfi
choosing-an-export-marketing-agency.h1: How a manufacturer should choose an export marketing agency
choosing-an-export-marketing-agency.description: Questions a Chinese manufacturer should ask before hiring an export marketing or SEO agency: guarantees, ownership, reporting, content and red flags.
choosing-an-export-marketing-agency.lead: Choosing an agency to help you sell abroad is a significant decision for a factory. A good agency will make your company easier to find and easier to trust. A poor one can waste a year and leave you with accounts you do not own. These are the questions we would ask, including of ourselves.

sections.h2: Start with the outcome you want
p: Before speaking to agencies, write down what success looks like in a year: more qualified RFQs from certain countries, a site that passes buyer checks, or less dependence on one marketplace. An agency should ask you this in the first meeting. If it starts with a package price instead, be careful.

Google’s own advice on [hiring an SEO](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/do-i-need-seo) states plainly that no one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google. An agency that guarantees rankings or a fixed number of leads is either measuring something meaningless or promising something it cannot control.
A good agency commits to work, process and honest reporting instead.
ul: Guaranteed first-page rankings
Guaranteed lead numbers regardless of product or price
Large volumes of “backlinks” for a fixed fee
Reports full of impressions and reach but no inquiries

p: Your domain, website, hosting account, Google Search Console, analytics and ad accounts should be registered to your company, with the agency given access. If you part ways, you keep the history and the assets.
ul: Domain registered in your company’s name
Search Console and analytics owned by your company account
Ad accounts in your name, with your payment method
Source files and content delivered to you

p: For a manufacturer, content quality depends on technical accuracy. Ask who writes product pages, how they learn your products and who approves technical claims. Google’s guidance on [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) suggests asking “Who, How, and Why” about each page; an agency should be able to answer those for the content it produces.

Mass-produced pages with little original information are a risk, not an asset. Google’s [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) describe practices such as scaled content abuse — many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings — and link spam.

Ask to see a sample report. The useful numbers for an exporter are qualified inquiries by source and market, search impressions and clicks for the products you care about, and the cost per qualified inquiry for paid campaigns.
Agree a monthly report and a quarterly review where the plan can change.

sections.h2: Start with a defined first scope
p: A sensible first project is small enough to judge: fixing the main product pages, building an RFQ path, or setting up search tracking. You will learn more about an agency from three months of real work than from any proposal.

sections.h2: Questions to ask before you sign
p: A short list of direct questions tells you more than a long sales deck. Ask every agency the same questions and compare the answers in writing.
ul: Who will do the work each month, and in which language do they write?
Which of these tasks are done by people, and which by software or AI tools?
What will you need from our engineers and sales team, and how much of their time?
Which reports will we get, and can we see an example from a similar engagement?
What happens to the website, domains, ad accounts and content if we stop working together?
How will you handle technical claims, certifications and safety statements?

p: Some warning signs come up again and again. Google’s spam policies describe link schemes and scaled content abuse — producing many pages mainly to manipulate rankings — as practices that can lead to lower rankings or removal from results. If a proposal promises hundreds of backlinks or “500 AI-written pages a month”, treat that as a risk, not a bonus.

Be cautious too of proposals that report only rankings for long lists of keywords nobody searches for, or traffic without inquiries. For a manufacturer, the useful numbers are qualified inquiries, RFQs and, eventually, orders.
ul: Guaranteed first-page rankings or a fixed number of leads.
Bulk link building or “private networks”.
Ownership of your domain or ad account held by the agency.
No access to the analytics and Search Console data.

sections.h2: How to compare two shortlisted agencies
p: When two agencies look similar, give each the same small paid task: for example, rewrite one key product page, or audit your top ten pages. Compare the quality of the work, how many questions they asked about your product, and how they handled technical details.

An agency that asks for datasheets, test reports and examples of real buyer questions is usually one that will write pages buyers trust. An agency that delivers quickly without asking anything has probably written something generic.

faq: Can any agency guarantee Google rankings?
No. Google states that no one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google. Treat guarantees as a warning sign.
Who should own our website and accounts?
Your company. The agency should have access, not ownership, so you keep everything if you change agency.
What should an agency report each month?
Qualified inquiries by source and market, search impressions and clicks for priority products, and spend and cost per inquiry for paid campaigns.
Is it a problem if an agency builds hundreds of pages quickly?
It can be. Pages with little original value can fall under Google’s spam policies on scaled content. Fewer, better pages are usually safer.
Should the agency understand our industry?
It should be willing to learn it and to work with your engineers. Ask how they will learn your products and who approves technical claims.
How long should the first contract be?
Long enough to do real work, short enough to judge. A defined first scope over a few months is reasonable.
Should we choose a Chinese agency or a foreign one?
Choose the one that can write naturally for your buyers and communicate well with your team. Ask to see English content they have written.
What are signs of a good agency?
They ask about your goals, admit what they cannot promise, put accounts in your name and show you real reporting.
How does Hurfi work?
We start with a free consultation, agree a scope, keep accounts in your name and report from them every month. We do not guarantee rankings or lead numbers.
svc: Sites built in your own hosting and domain, with source files handed over.
SEO reported from your own Search Console, with no ranking guarantees.
Ad accounts in your company name, reported by cost per qualified inquiry.
LinkedIn pages owned by your company, with the agency as an admin.
extra_claims: No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google.
Google suggests asking Who, How and Why about content.
Google spam policies include scaled content abuse and link spam.
Scaled content abuse: many pages generated primarily to manipulate rankings; sites violating spam policies may rank lower or not appear.

linkedin-for-factory-export-sales.title: LinkedIn for Factory Export Sales: A Practical Guide | Hurfi
linkedin-for-factory-export-sales.h1: LinkedIn for factory export sales: a practical guide
linkedin-for-factory-export-sales.description: How Chinese manufacturers can use LinkedIn company pages and sales profiles to support export sales: setup, content, outreach and measurement.
linkedin-for-factory-export-sales.lead: When a factory’s sales manager emails an overseas buyer, the buyer often looks up the person and the company on LinkedIn before replying. A blank or inconsistent profile costs trust. This guide covers what a manufacturer needs on LinkedIn and how to keep it working without fabricating anything.

sections.h2: Why LinkedIn matters to overseas buyers
p: LinkedIn is where many procurement and engineering staff check a supplier and the person contacting them. They look for consistency: does the company page match the website, does the salesperson work there, and is there evidence of real production?
A LinkedIn presence does not replace a website. It is a second place to check you, and it should point to the website for details.

sections.h2: Set up the company page properly
p: LinkedIn Help explains how to [create a LinkedIn Page](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a543852) for a company. Use your English company name exactly as it appears on your website and documents, your website URL, your real location and a short description of what you make.
ul: Logo and cover image you own
Description that names your products and the industries you serve
Website link to the English site
Location matching your factory address
At least two admins from your company

p: Each person who contacts buyers should have a profile with their real name, a professional photo, their role and the company page linked as their employer. Buyers notice when a salesperson’s profile is empty or lists a different company.

sections.h2: Post what only your factory can show
p: The most useful posts show things buyers cannot see elsewhere: a new line being installed, a test being run, an engineer explaining a design choice, packaging for an export order (without client names). One genuine post a week beats daily generic content.
ul: Production and testing photos or short videos you own
Trade-show dates and booth details for confirmed fairs
Certifications when you receive them, with scope
Introductions to engineers and sales staff
Links to new product pages on your website

p: Connection requests and messages work best when they are specific: why you are contacting this person, what you make that is relevant to them, and a link to the right product page. Mass messages with no context damage your reputation and can restrict your account.
Track replies, meetings and RFQs that started on LinkedIn, and visits from LinkedIn to your website in analytics. Follower counts are less important than whether the right buyers engage.

sections.h2: A weekly routine for a small export team
p: LinkedIn works best as a steady habit, not a campaign. For a factory with one or two export sales staff, an hour or two a week is enough if it is spent on the right things.
ul: **Monday:** post one piece of factory content — a production step, a test, a shipment — with a short explanation in English.
**Tuesday–Thursday:** reply to comments and messages within a working day; accept relevant connection requests.
**Weekly:** send a few personalised messages to buyers or engineers who engaged with your posts or visited your profile.
**Monthly:** review which posts led to profile visits, website clicks or conversations, and do more of those.

sections.h2: What to post when you cannot show customers
p: Many factories cannot name customers or show their parts. That does not leave you with nothing to post. Buyers want to see process, quality and people, and you can show those without revealing a client.
ul: Inspection equipment in use, with what it measures and how often.
Before-and-after examples of a process improvement, without customer names.
Certification audits passed, new equipment installed, capacity added.
Short explanations of a material, tolerance or standard your buyers ask about.
Your team: the engineer who answers technical questions, the person who handles shipping.

p: Every LinkedIn post should have somewhere to go. Link to the matching product or capability page on your website, not just the home page. On the website, make the RFQ form short and clear, so a buyer who clicks through from LinkedIn can ask a question in a minute.
Use tagged links (UTM parameters) on the links you post, so your analytics show which LinkedIn posts lead to visits and inquiries. Without that, it is hard to tell whether LinkedIn is working.

sections.h2: Mistakes that make factories look unreliable
ul: A company page with no logo, no website link or a description copied from a marketplace.
Sales profiles with different company names, job titles in Chinese only, or no photo.
Connection requests followed immediately by a price list.
Posting only product photos with “best price, contact us”, and nothing about process or quality.
Long gaps between posts, so the page looks abandoned when a buyer checks it.
p2: Each of these is easy to fix, and fixing them matters because buyers check LinkedIn to confirm that a supplier is real before they reply.

faq: Do B2B buyers really use LinkedIn to check suppliers?
Many procurement and engineering staff do, especially before replying to someone they do not know. A consistent profile reduces doubt.
Should we create a company page or only personal profiles?
Both. The company page shows the organisation; personal profiles show who buyers will deal with. Link them.
What should we post?
Real production, testing, engineering and team content you own, plus new products with links to your website. Avoid stock images and generic slogans.
How often should we post?
Regularly enough to look active — often one genuine post a week is enough for a factory.
Can we buy followers or connections?
No. Fake followers do not buy anything and can damage trust if noticed.
Can we use LinkedIn in China?
Access depends on your network setup and LinkedIn’s services in your region. Many export teams manage their pages from outside China or through partners.

Hidden text or keyword lists aimed at AI systems
Claims that a special file or markup is required to appear

google-ads-for-exporters.description: How Chinese manufacturers can set up Google Ads for overseas B2B inquiries: location targeting, keywords, landing pages, conversion tracking and budgets.
google-ads-for-exporters.lead: Google Ads can bring overseas buyers to a factory’s website within days, but it can also spend a budget on the wrong countries and the wrong searches. This guide covers the settings and checks that matter most for B2B exporters.

sections.h2: Set up conversion tracking before spending
p: Decide what counts as a conversion: an RFQ form submission, a quote request email or a WhatsApp click. Track them in Google Analytics and import them into Google Ads. Google Analytics lists [recommended events](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9267735) for lead generation, including generate_lead for when a user submits a form or request.

Without conversion tracking you cannot tell which keywords bring buyers, and automated bidding has nothing to learn from. Google Ads Help states that to use [Smart Bidding](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7065882) you need conversion tracking enabled, and some strategies rely on a minimum volume of conversion data.

Google Ads offers advanced [location options](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1722043). The broad setting, “Presence or Interest”, reaches people in your target locations and people who have shown interest in them; “Presence” limits ads to people who are in or regularly in those locations.

For an exporter, it is worth checking which setting fits. Google notes that the location mentioned in a search is considered first. Review the location report after the first weeks and exclude places you cannot serve.
ul: Target the countries where you can ship, certify and support
Exclude mainland China if your campaign is for overseas buyers only
Check the location report and adjust

p: Broad product words attract consumers, students and competitors. Specific searches — product plus specification, standard, “manufacturer”, “supplier” or “OEM” — are more likely to come from buyers. Add negative keywords for retail, “free”, “DIY” and job searches.

sections.h2: Send clicks to the right page
p: Each ad group should lead to the product page that matches the search, with specifications, proof and an RFQ form. Sending every click to the home page wastes money; the buyer has to search again.

sections.h2: Start small and measure cost per qualified inquiry
p: Begin with a test budget on a few products and markets. After a few weeks, judge results by the number of qualified inquiries and what each one cost — not by clicks or impressions. The search terms report shows the actual searches that triggered your ads. Review it weekly at first, add negatives and move good terms into their own ad groups.

Google Ads offers broad geo targeting, called “Presence or Interest”, which reaches people in your target locations and also people who have shown interest in them. Google recommends broad targeting as a best practice on Search, but says to consider “Presence” when you only want to reach users in specific locations, not users elsewhere who are interested in them.

Exporters who can only serve buyers in certain countries — because of certification, voltage, shipping or distributor agreements — often fit that second case. Whichever setting you choose, check the location report after a few weeks and adjust based on where qualified inquiries actually come from.

Industrial searches attract many clicks you do not want: job seekers, students, consumers looking for one unit, and people looking for repairs. A negative keyword list stops those searches triggering your ads.
ul: Job and education terms: job, jobs, career, salary, course, training, PDF.
Consumer terms, if you do not sell single units: for home, DIY, near me, price of one.
Repair and second-hand terms, unless you offer those services: repair, used, second hand.

p: Set up a conversion for each meaningful action: RFQ form submissions, contact form submissions, email clicks and WhatsApp or phone clicks. In Google Analytics 4, the recommended event for a submitted form or request for information is generate_lead.

Then judge campaigns by cost per qualified inquiry, not cost per click. A campaign with expensive clicks that brings two real RFQs a month is better than a cheap campaign that brings none. Review leads with your sales team each month and mark which ones were real buyers.

Start with a budget you can sustain for at least two to three months, focused on one or two markets and a few product groups. Industrial buyers search less often than consumers, so it takes time to collect enough data to judge a campaign.

Consider buyers’ time zones and working days when you review results, and make sure someone can answer inquiries quickly in those hours. An ad that brings an RFQ at 9 a.m. in Germany is wasted if the reply comes two days later.

industrial-product-page-seo.title: Industrial Product Page SEO: What Buyers and Google Need | Hurfi
industrial-product-page-seo.h1: Product page SEO for industrial manufacturers
industrial-product-page-seo.description: How to structure industrial product pages so overseas engineers and Google understand them: titles, specifications, documents, compliance and structured data.
industrial-product-page-seo.lead: For a manufacturer, the product page does most of the selling. It is where an engineer decides whether to send an RFQ, and where Google decides whether the page answers a search. This guide covers what a good industrial product page contains.

p: The title should say what the product is in the buyer’s words, with the most important specification or variant: for example “Stainless steel ball valve, DN15–DN100, PN40” rather than “Product 3”. Google’s [SEO Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide) recommends descriptive titles and notes that Google does not use the keywords meta tag.

Engineers search for numbers: sizes, ratings, tolerances, materials, standards. If those numbers are only in an image or a PDF, they are harder for buyers to scan and for search engines to read. Publish a specification table on the page and keep the PDF as a download.
ul: Units and test conditions next to every value
Variants in one table rather than separate thin pages
Materials and finishes with the standards they meet
Drawings or dimension diagrams you own

p: Say where the product is used and where it should not be used. Application text helps buyers who search by problem rather than by product name, and honest limits build trust with engineers.

List certificates for the product and market, with the holder and scope. For products sold in the EU that need CE marking, the [European Commission](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/ce-marking_en) explains that the manufacturer carries out the conformity assessment, sets up the technical file, issues the EU declaration of conformity and affixes the marking. Only claim what you hold.

sections.h2: Use structured data that matches the page
p: Google’s [Product structured data](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/product) documentation describes two types: Product snippets for pages that are not purchase pages, and merchant listings for pages where a product can be bought. Most B2B product pages fit the first. Mark up only what is visible on the page.

Every product page should end with a short form or a clear contact: what the buyer needs (quantity, specification, market, date) and who will answer. Track submissions by page so you know which products bring inquiries.

sections.h2: A product page outline you can reuse
p: Most industrial product pages work well with the same basic outline. It gives buyers what they need in the order they look for it, and gives search engines clear text to work with.
ol: **Title and one-line summary:** what the product is, its key specification and who it is for.
**Key specifications table:** in HTML, with units, tolerances and test conditions.
**Applications:** where it is used, and where it should not be used.
**Materials, options and customisation:** what can be changed and what cannot.
**Compliance and documents:** certificates, test reports and datasheets, with their scope.
**Packaging, MOQ and lead time:** typical ranges, clearly stated as such.
**RFQ path:** a short form or contact link with what information to include.

sections.h2: How to handle hundreds of variants
p: Industrial products often come in many sizes, materials and ratings. Creating a page for every variant usually produces hundreds of near-identical pages that do not help buyers and may be treated as low value.

A better approach is one strong page per product family, with a variant table and filters. Create separate pages only for variants that buyers search for by name, or that have different applications, certifications or documents. Link variant pages back to the family page, and make sure each one has something unique to say.

sections.h2: Common mistakes on factory product pages
ul: Specifications only in images or PDFs, so they cannot be searched or copied.
Titles that are only a model number, with no description of the product.
Copying a competitor’s or a marketplace description word for word.
Vague claims such as “high quality” and “best price” instead of measured values.
CE or other marks shown without saying which directives or standards apply.
No visible way to ask a question or request a quote.

sections.h2: Who should review a product page
p: Product pages carry technical and legal weight. A wrong tolerance or an overstated certification can cost an order or create liability. Before a page is published, an engineer should check the specifications and applications, someone responsible for quality should check compliance statements, and a sales person should check that the page answers the questions buyers ask most.
Record who reviewed each page and when. When a specification or certificate changes, update the page and the date, so buyers and search engines see current information.

faq: What makes an industrial product page rank?
Clear relevance to the search — a descriptive title, specifications in text, application content — plus a site that is crawlable, fast and trusted.
Should every variant have its own page?
Usually not. Group minor variants in a table on one page. Give separate pages to products that buyers search for separately.
Are PDF datasheets bad for SEO?
Not bad, but not enough. Put the key specifications on the HTML page and offer the PDF too.
Does Google use the keywords meta tag?
No. Google states that it does not use the keywords meta tag.
Which structured data should B2B product pages use?
Usually Product snippets markup, which Google describes for non-purchase pages. Mark up only what is visible.
Can we list CE or other certificates?
Yes, if you hold them for that product. Name the product, scope and holder. The manufacturer is responsible for CE conformity assessment.
Should we show prices?
For configured or custom products, often not. Explain what affects price and invite an RFQ.
How long should a product page be?
As long as it needs to answer the buyer’s questions. Specifications, applications, compliance and an RFQ form usually take more than a paragraph.
Can Hurfi write our product pages?
Yes. We draft them from your documents with your engineers and you approve every technical statement.

trade-show-follow-up-for-manufacturers.description: How manufacturers can turn Canton Fair and trade-show contacts into RFQs: preparation, the website buyers check afterwards, follow-up timing and tracking.
trade-show-follow-up-for-manufacturers.lead: Trade shows still bring many factories their best buyers. But most of the work happens after the fair, when buyers compare dozens of suppliers they met. This guide covers how to make sure the follow-up — and the website buyers check — works in your favour.

sections.h2: Why the follow-up matters more than the booth
p: At a large fair, a buyer may visit many booths in a day. Afterwards, they sort the contacts: who made what they need, who replied clearly, and who looks trustworthy online. The supplier that follows up fastest with useful information often gets the RFQ.

The [Canton Fair](https://www.cantonfair.org.cn/en-US/about), for example, has been held in Guangzhou every spring and autumn since 1957. Many buyers attend repeatedly and keep comparing suppliers between sessions.

sections.h2: Prepare your website before the fair
ul: Product pages for every item you will exhibit, with specifications in text
A trade-show page with booth details for confirmed fairs, linking to those products
An English contact page with the names of the people at the booth
A short URL or QR code on brochures that leads to the right product section
An RFQ form that works on phones

sections.h2: Capture useful details at the booth
p: Record more than a business card: which products the buyer looked at, their market, quantity, timing and any certification needs. These notes make the follow-up specific instead of generic.

sections.h2: Follow up within days, with the right link
p: Send a short email that reminds the buyer who you are, answers the question they asked and links to the exact product page — not only the home page or a large catalogue. Buyers who search your company name after the fair should find your own website first.

sections.h2: Track every contact through to RFQ
p: Use a simple CRM or spreadsheet: contact, product interest, date of follow-up, reply, RFQ, quote. Tag website visits from fair materials (for example with campaign parameters on QR links) so you can see which fair brought which inquiries.

Buyers who were not ready to order may be ready months later. Useful updates — new products, certifications, a short video of a line — keep you on their list. LinkedIn helps here too, as a second place buyers can follow and check you.

sections.h2: A follow-up email template that works
p: The first email after a fair should be short, specific and easy to reply to. Mention where you met, what the visitor asked about, and give one clear next step.
ul: **Subject:** name of the fair, your company and the product discussed.
**First line:** where and when you met, and what they were interested in.
**Middle:** a link to the exact product or capability page, plus one answer to their question.
**Next step:** a specific offer — samples, a quotation, a short video call — with a date.
**Signature:** name, role, direct email, WhatsApp or phone, and website.
**Days 1–3:** first email to every qualified contact, with the right page link.
**Days 7–10:** second touch for those who did not reply: a short note with something useful, such as a datasheet or a case without client names.
**Days 14–21:** connect on LinkedIn with a personal note; send quotations or samples to those who asked.
**Day 30:** review every contact — active, paused or not a fit — and record the reason.

sections.h2: Measuring the return on a fair
p: Booth costs, travel and samples add up. To judge whether a fair is worth repeating, track a few numbers for each one: qualified contacts, follow-ups sent, RFQs received, quotations sent and orders won, with the value of each.

Tag the links in your follow-up emails so your analytics show which fair contacts visited your site and which pages they read. Over two or three fairs, this tells you which events, products and messages bring real buyers.

A fair gives you a few days with buyers each year; your website works the other 360. After each fair, add what you learned: answers to the most common booth questions, pages for products that drew interest, and photos or short videos of new equipment.
Buyers who could not attend — or who found you later through a colleague — will look at your site first. If it reflects what you showed at the fair, it continues the conversation the booth started.

faq: How soon should we follow up after a trade show?
Within days, while the buyer still remembers your booth. Answer their question and link to the exact product page.
What should a follow-up email include?
A reminder of who you are, the answer to the buyer’s question, a link to the matching product page, and one clear next step.
Why does our website matter after the fair?
Buyers compare suppliers afterwards and often search your company name. Your site should confirm what they saw at the booth.
When is the Canton Fair held?
According to the organiser, every spring and autumn in Guangzhou. It was first held in spring 1957.
Should we make a separate page for each fair?
One trade-show page, updated with confirmed fairs and linking to products, is usually enough. Separate thin pages per fair add little.
How do we track which fair brought an order?
Tag QR links and fair-specific URLs with campaign parameters, and record each contact in a CRM or sheet through to RFQ.
Should we connect with buyers on LinkedIn after the fair?
Yes, with a personal note mentioning the fair and product. Keep your company page consistent with your website.
What if buyers do not reply?
Send one or two useful follow-ups with new information, then keep in touch occasionally. Avoid repetitive messages.

Yes. We can prepare product pages, the trade-show page, tracking links and follow-up templates.

export-website-speed-for-overseas-buyers.title: Export Website Speed: Why It Matters to Overseas Buyers | Hurfi
export-website-speed-for-overseas-buyers.h1: Export website speed: making pages fast for overseas buyers
export-website-speed-for-overseas-buyers.description: Why page speed matters for Chinese exporters’ websites, what Core Web Vitals measure, and practical fixes for hosting, images and scripts.
export-website-speed-for-overseas-buyers.lead: Many Chinese factory websites are fast inside China and slow everywhere else. For an overseas buyer on a phone, a slow product page is often the last page they see. This guide explains what to measure and the fixes that usually help most.

p: Buyers abroad reach your site over international connections. If the server is in mainland China or the page loads large images and many scripts, the wait can be long. Google’s guidance on [page experience](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/page-experience) explains that it looks at signals such as Core Web Vitals alongside content relevance.
[Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) defines three core metrics and their “good” thresholds:
ul: Largest Contentful Paint (loading): 2.5 seconds or less
Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness): 200 milliseconds or less
Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability): 0.1 or less
p2: Measure these from the countries where your buyers are, on mobile as well as desktop.

p: For an export site, hosting outside mainland China, or using a content delivery network with servers near your markets, usually makes the biggest difference. Keep a separate Chinese site in China if you need one for domestic buyers.

ul: Use modern formats such as WebP
Resize images to the size they are displayed
Set width and height so the layout does not jump
Lazy-load images below the first screen
Replace heavy sliders with one clear image

p: Chat widgets, tracking scripts, web fonts and video embeds add weight. Keep the ones you use and remove the rest. Scripts or fonts served from services that are slow or blocked in some regions can delay the whole page.
Use Lighthouse or PageSpeed tools on your key product pages, fix the largest problems first and test again. Check Search Console’s Core Web Vitals report over time for real-user data.

web.dev gives clear targets for Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) of 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) of 0.1 or less.

It also recommends measuring at the 75th percentile of page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. In practice this means most of your real visitors should get a good experience — not just you, testing from the office on a fast connection.

sections.h2: Test from where your buyers are
p: A site that loads quickly in Shenzhen may be slow in Frankfurt or São Paulo, because of where it is hosted and how assets are delivered. Test key pages from the regions you sell to, using tools that let you choose a test location, and on mobile as well as desktop.

Chrome Lighthouse, which Google mentions as a tool for page-experience improvements, is useful for finding problems on a single page. Real-user data, when available, shows what visitors actually experience over time.
ul: Test your home page, a top product page and the RFQ page.
Test from at least two target regions, on mobile and desktop.
Record results before and after each change, so you know what helped.
Convert large JPEG and PNG product photos to WebP or AVIF, sized to how they are displayed.
Set width and height on images so the layout does not jump as they load.
Lazy-load images below the first screen; do not lazy-load the main image.
Remove unused plugins, sliders, chat widgets and tracking scripts.
Replace auto-playing background videos with a still image and an optional play button.
Use a CDN with locations near your buyers for images, CSS and JavaScript.

p: Speed tends to slip over time as new images, plugins and tracking scripts are added. Set a simple rule: every new page is checked before it is published, and the key pages are re-tested every quarter from your main buyer regions.

Write down a few limits your team can follow — for example, a maximum image width and file size, no auto-playing video, and no new third-party script without a reason. Small rules like these keep a fast site fast.

faq: Does website speed affect Google rankings?
Google uses page experience signals, including Core Web Vitals, alongside relevance. Speed alone will not rank a page, but slow pages lose buyers.
What are good Core Web Vitals values?
web.dev gives LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, INP of 200 milliseconds or less and CLS of 0.1 or less as good.
Our site is fast in China. Why is it slow abroad?
Often because of server location, international connections, or scripts and fonts that load slowly outside China. Test from your target countries.
Should we host our export site outside China?
For most exporters, yes, or use a CDN with servers near your markets.
What is the quickest fix?
Usually images: compress them, convert to WebP and size them correctly.
Do chat widgets slow sites down?
They can. Keep only the tools you actually use.
How do we measure real-user speed?
Search Console’s Core Web Vitals report shows field data when enough visits are recorded.
Does speed matter for B2B buyers?
Yes. Buyers often research on phones and between meetings, and they have many other suppliers to check.

china-export-markets-2025.h1: Where Chinese manufacturing exports grew and fell in 2025 — and what it means for your website
china-export-markets-2025.description: What 2025 provincial and city statistical bulletins show about export growth and decline by market, and how exporters can plan market pages from it.
china-export-markets-2025.lead: Official 2025 statistical bulletins tell a clear story: exports to the United States fell in many places, while sales to the EU, ASEAN and Africa grew in several provinces and cities. This guide pulls together the figures we checked for our location guides and explains what they mean for an export website.

p: Each Chinese province and city publishes an annual statistical bulletin (统计公报) with goods trade, exports and, often, exports by market. We use them because they are official and comparable. They describe whole regions, not your company: use them for context, then check your own orders and inquiries.
Several inland provinces reported strong export growth in 2025:
ul: Hubei: exports up 19.6% to 581.86 billion yuan, with trade with the EU up 40.2%.
Henan: exports up 18.0% to 616.818 billion yuan.
Anhui: exports up 17.8% to 682.31 billion yuan; trade with ASEAN up 38.3% and with the EU 21.6%.
p2: Much of this was driven by vehicles, batteries and electronics. Anhui’s bulletin, for example, reports vehicle exports of 1.228 million units and exports of electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries and solar products up 107.8%.

p: Other bulletins show declines:
ul: Fujian: exports down 6.7% to 1,155.362 billion yuan, with exports to the United States down 22.1% and to ASEAN 18.0% — but exports to the EU up 9.7%.
Fuzhou: exports down 32.0% to 174.73 billion yuan, falling in the US, EU and ASEAN.
Hunan: exports down 4.1%; exports to the United States down 29.2%, while exports to ASEAN rose 5.5%.
Sichuan: exports down 1.5% to 608.65 billion yuan.

sections.h2: The United States fell, other markets grew
p: City bulletins that list markets show the same pattern again and again:
ul: Nantong: exports to the EU up 20.7%, ASEAN 20.9% and Africa 15.8%; to the United States down 19.3%.
Taizhou (Zhejiang): exports to the EU up 6.3%; to the United States down 14.4%.
Ningde: exports to the EU up 66.4%; to the United States down 13.5%.
p2: For many exporters, the question in 2026 is not whether to look beyond the United States, but which markets to prepare for first.

p: Regional figures do not tell you where your products sell. Before you plan anything, look at your own last two years:
ul: Orders and revenue by country.
Website inquiries and RFQs by country.
Searches and clicks by country in Search Console.
Which countries ask for samples but do not order — and why.

sections.h2: Pick two or three markets you can really serve
p: A market is worth a page only if you can meet its rules and serve its buyers. For each candidate, ask:
ul: Do we hold the certifications this market requires?
Can we quote the delivery terms buyers there expect?
Can we answer inquiries in time, in a language they use?
Do we have at least a few customers or references there?

sections.h2: Prepare the rules before the page
p: For the EU, for example, the European Commission explains that manufacturers must carry out the conformity assessment, prepare the technical file, issue the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking where it applies ([CE marking](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/ce-marking_en)). sections.h2: Build market pages that help buyers
p: Good market pages are specific: the products you sell there, the standards and certificates that apply, the delivery terms you offer, references in the region and who will answer. Google’s guidance on [managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) explains the URL and language options if you add translated versions.

Track inquiries by market from the first week. After three to six months you will know which markets respond and which need different products, prices or terms. Statistics point the way; your own data decides.

Do these figures predict my sales?

Should we stop selling to the United States?
That is a business decision we cannot make for you. Many exporters are adding markets rather than leaving one.
Which markets should we target next?
The ones where you hold the right certifications, can quote the right terms and already have some customers or interest.
How many market pages should we build?
Start with two or three strong ones. Thin pages for every country rarely help buyers or search.
Do we need translated sites?
Only where buyers prefer another language and you can answer them in it.
Can Hurfi guarantee results in new markets?
No. Nobody can. We plan carefully and report honestly from your own data.

This guide explains how to build market pages that answer them — and how to avoid pages that only exist for search engines.

p: Several 2025 bulletins show growth in these markets. Nantong’s exports to ASEAN rose 20.9% and to Africa 15.8%. Hunan’s exports to ASEAN rose 5.5% while its exports to the United States fell 29.2%. Weifang made 62% of its trade with Belt and Road countries, and Hubei 54.9%.

sections.h2: What buyers in these markets ask
p: Questions vary by country and product, but some come up again and again:
ul: Can you deliver to my port or city, and on what terms?
Do you have distributors, service partners or spare parts nearby?
Which certifications or registrations does my country require, and do you hold them?
Can you supply in smaller quantities to start?
Can I talk to someone in my language or time zone?

References or projects in the region you are allowed to show.

p: Google’s [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) describe doorway abuse: pages created to rank for similar searches that lead users to less useful intermediate pages, including pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page. Buyers far away need more proof, not less. Show real factory photos, testing, packing and loading; dated references in the region; and certificates with scope and validity. Avoid stock photos and claims you cannot support.

Add the page to your XML sitemap.

Contact and RFQ form.

No. Build strong pages for the markets you really serve. Thin, repeated country pages can count as doorway abuse under Google’s spam policies.
Is English enough for the Middle East and Africa?
Often for B2B, but Arabic or French pages can help in some markets — if you can answer inquiries in those languages.

An annotation that tells Google which pages are language or regional versions of each other, so it can show the right one.
Do we need local certifications?

Should we show prices for these markets?
Usually not exact prices, but MOQs, terms and lead times help buyers decide.
Can Hurfi translate our pages?
We plan and build language versions with proper translation and correct tags, and we review them with you.
Can you guarantee rankings in these markets?
No. Nobody can. We report honestly from your own Search Console.

certifications-page-for-export-websites.title: The Certifications Page Export Buyers Look For | Hurfi
certifications-page-for-export-websites.h1: The certifications page: how exporters should present certificates to overseas buyers
certifications-page-for-export-websites.description: How Chinese manufacturers can present certifications by market on their website — scope, models, validity and documents — without overclaiming.
certifications-page-for-export-websites.lead: For many overseas buyers, certifications are the first filter: no right certificate, no RFQ. Yet many factory websites show a wall of logos with no detail. This guide explains how to build a certifications page that buyers trust, and how to link it to your products.

sections.h2: Why certifications decide the first call
p: A buyer in Europe, North America or the Middle East usually has to prove that what they import meets local rules. Before contacting you, they want to know whether your products already comply. If your site does not say, the easiest decision is to move on to a supplier whose site does.

sections.h2: What the EU expects from manufacturers
p: The European Commission’s [CE marking page](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/ce-marking_en) explains that manufacturers are responsible for carrying out the conformity assessment, setting up the technical file, issuing the EU declaration of conformity and affixing the CE marking. Importers and distributors must make sure the products they place on the market meet the rules.
This is why European buyers ask for your declaration of conformity and test reports: their own responsibility depends on yours.
A list of logos is hard to use. Group your certificates by the market or buyer they matter to:
ul: European Union: CE-related declarations and test reports, and other EU requirements that apply to your products.
Other markets you sell to: the certificates or registrations each requires, as confirmed by the relevant authority.
Quality and management systems: ISO or industry-specific certificates.
China: compulsory certification (CCC) and other domestic approvals where relevant.
Certificate name and number.
Issuing body or test laboratory.
Scope: which products and models it covers.
Issue and expiry dates.
A downloadable copy or the option to request one.

p: Only list certificates you hold, for the products they really cover. Do not imply that a quality-system certificate is a product certificate, or that a test report is a certification. A buyer who finds one overstatement will doubt everything else — and in regulated markets it can create legal problems for both of you.

On every product page, say which certificates cover that product and link to the certifications page. On the certifications page, link back to the products. Buyers then see compliance in context, and search engines see clear relationships between pages.
Where it fits the page and the information is accurate, [Product structured data](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/product) can describe your products to Google.

Certificates expire, scopes change and new models need testing. Give one person the job of checking the page every quarter. An expired certificate on your website tells a buyer you are not paying attention.
Some documents you may not want to publish openly. Offer them on request with a short form: the buyer’s company, market and products of interest. That request is itself a strong sales lead.

Most manufacturers can use the same structure: a short introduction, then one block per market, then quality-system certificates, then a “request documents” form. Inside each market block, a table works well:
ul: Column 1: certificate or document name.
Column 2: products and models covered.
Column 3: issuing body or laboratory.
Column 4: valid until.
Column 5: download or request link.
p2: Keep the table in HTML, not as an image, so buyers can search it and read it on a phone.

ul: Logos of certification marks the company does not hold.
Certificates issued to a different company, such as a trading partner, without saying so.
Expired certificates still shown as current.
Test reports presented as certifications.
Scanned certificates so blurred that the number cannot be read.

sections.h2: Write it for people, not only for search
p: Google’s guidance on [helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) applies here too. A clear page that answers a buyer’s compliance questions is more useful — and more convincing — than a page of keywords.

faq: Should we show certificate logos?
You can, but always with the details: number, issuer, scope and validity. Logos alone do not answer buyers’ questions.
Who is responsible for CE marking?
The European Commission explains that the manufacturer carries out the conformity assessment, prepares the technical file, issues the declaration of conformity and affixes the CE marking.
Can we publish test reports?
You can publish them or offer them on request. Make clear which products and models they cover.
We hold ISO 9001. Is that a product certificate?
No. It certifies a quality-management system. Present it as that, separately from product certifications.
Do we need a page per certificate?
Usually one certifications page grouped by market is enough, plus the relevant certificates on each product page.
How often should we update it?
At least every quarter, and whenever a certificate is issued, renewed or expires.
Can Hurfi tell us which certificates we need?
No. That is for your compliance team, test laboratories or authorities. We help you present what you hold clearly and accurately.

shipping-logistics-page-for-exporters.h1: The shipping and logistics page: answering buyers’ delivery questions before they ask
shipping-logistics-page-for-exporters.description: What a Chinese manufacturer’s shipping page should cover — Incoterms, ports, packing, lead times and samples — so overseas buyers can plan and request a quote.
shipping-logistics-page-for-exporters.lead: “Which port? Which terms? How long?” Almost every overseas buyer asks these questions, often before asking about price. A clear shipping and logistics page answers them once, builds confidence and saves your sales team many emails. This guide explains what to include.

p: A buyer has to land your product at their door at a known cost and on a known date. If they cannot work that out, they cannot compare you with other suppliers. A shipping page turns an unknown into something they can plan.

The International Chamber of Commerce describes the [Incoterms® rules](https://iccwbo.org/business-solutions/incoterms-rules/) as eleven three-letter trade terms that clarify the tasks, costs and risks involved in delivering goods from sellers to buyers. Say which terms you usually offer and name the version you use, for example Incoterms® 2020.
Do not list every term if you only quote two or three. Be clear about what you will and will not arrange.

Tell buyers where goods leave China. Many manufacturers ship through large container ports — Jiaxing’s port, for example, handled 4.255 million TEU in 2025 and Fujian’s ports 18.4364 million TEU. Inland suppliers should explain how goods reach the coast or travel by rail.
ul: Main port(s) of loading.
Rail or river routes if you use them.
Air freight for samples or urgent orders.
Typical transit times to your main markets, as ranges.
Standard export packing for each product family.
Pallet, crate or carton options and dimensions.
Container loading: how many units per 20′ or 40′ container, if useful.
Marking, labelling and documents that travel with the goods.

p: Give ranges for standard products, custom products and repeat orders, and say what affects them: materials, tooling, testing or season. Buyers trust realistic ranges more than promises that turn out to be wrong.
Many relationships start with a sample. Explain how buyers can get one, what it costs, how it is shipped and how long it takes. If you accept small trial orders, say so and give the minimum.

List the export documents you routinely supply, and explain how you handle special cases such as oversized machinery or goods that need dangerous-goods handling. Do not claim capabilities you do not have; say instead which forwarders or partners you work with.

sections.h2: Link it from every product page
p: Put a short “Shipping and lead times” line on each product page with a link to the full page. Add the shipping page to your main navigation or footer and to your XML sitemap. A buyer should never have to search for it.

ul: Ports of loading and any inland routes.
Incoterms you usually quote, with the version.
Packing by product family, with photos.
Lead-time ranges for samples, standard and custom orders.
Documents you supply with each shipment.
Who to contact for a freight quote.
p2: If you can tick every item, most buyers will have the information they need to compare you and ask for a quote.

sections.h2: Show it, do not just say it
p: Photos and short videos of packing, loading and containers leaving your factory are some of the most convincing content an exporter can publish. They show care, capacity and that you really ship — things buyers cannot judge from text alone.
Freight rates and transit times change. Avoid quoting fixed prices; give the information that stays stable — ports, terms, packing and ranges — and invite buyers to request a current quote.

faq: What are Incoterms?
The ICC describes them as eleven three-letter trade terms that clarify the tasks, costs and risks in delivering goods from seller to buyer.
Should we publish freight prices?
Usually not. Rates change. Publish ports, terms, packing and lead-time ranges, and quote freight on request.
We are an inland supplier. What should we say?
Explain how goods reach the port or travel by rail, and give realistic transit times.
Should the shipping page list every Incoterm?
No. List the terms you usually offer and name the version.
Do buyers care about packing?
Yes, especially for machinery, fragile goods and long routes. Photos of real packing help.
Where should the page appear?
In the navigation or footer, linked from every product page, and in your sitemap.
Can Hurfi write this page for us?
Yes. We draft it from your team’s information and your logistics staff approve every detail.

standing-out-in-an-industrial-cluster.description: How manufacturers in Chinese industrial clusters — pumps, fabrics, wigs, eyewear — can make their website stand out from hundreds of similar suppliers.
standing-out-in-an-industrial-cluster.lead: In many Chinese cities, hundreds of factories make the same kind of product. A buyer searching for pumps, printed fabric or wigs will find dozens of suppliers that look alike. This guide explains how to make your website the one they contact.

sections.h2: Answer questions before they are asked
ul: MOQ and sample terms.

Certifications by market.

p: Google’s guidance on [helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether content provides original information and substantial value compared with other pages. In a cluster, original content means your own products, data and photos — not text copied from a neighbour’s site or a marketplace listing.

sections.h2: Use the cluster as context, not as your message
p: Being in a well-known production city can reassure buyers about supply chains and experience. Mention it, but do not make it your main message: every competitor can say the same.
Open your home page and a competitor’s side by side. Cover the logos. If a buyer could not tell which is which, your site is not yet doing its job. Then ask:
ul: Does our first screen say what we make that is different?
Can a buyer find a specification table in two clicks?
Are the photos clearly from our factory?
Do we answer MOQ, lead time and certification questions without an email?
p2: Each “no” is a place to start.

p: In a cluster, specialists often win online: the supplier that makes one kind of pump, fabric or wig very well, and says so clearly. If you have a speciality, put it first. If you make a broad range, organise it so that each family has the depth a specialist would show.

sections.h2: Measure what makes buyers contact you
p: Track which pages lead to inquiries. Over time you will see which differences buyers care about, and you can strengthen those pages first.

Is it worth naming our city?

How many products should we put online?
Start with the families that bring the best inquiries, and make those pages excellent.
Do we need our own photos?
Yes. Stock or supplier photos make you look like a trader.
Can marketplaces replace our website?
Marketplaces can bring inquiries, but your own site is where you can show everything that makes you different.
Can Hurfi guarantee we outrank competitors?
No. Nobody can. We build better pages and report honestly from your own data.

sections.h2: Write titles that match the product
p: Google’s guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive and concise text in each page’s title element. Use the product type and its main specification, not just a model code.

Where it fits and the facts are accurate, [Product structured data](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/product) can describe your products to Google. Google’s documentation describes product snippets for pages where people cannot directly purchase the product — the situation of most B2B product pages.

Imagine a 120-page pump catalogue with 15 series and 400 models. Instead of one PDF, the website gets 15 series pages, each with a model table, curves, materials, certificates and a datasheet download. Category pages group the series by application. The PDF stays available for buyers who want it.
The buyer searching for a specific type of pump now lands on the right series page, compares models in a table and sends an RFQ from that page — and you know which series it came from.

faq: Can Google index our PDF catalogue?
Yes, Google can index PDFs. But product pages usually serve buyers and search better than one long catalogue.
Should we remove the PDF?
No. Keep it as a download, and keep it consistent with the product pages.
How many pages do we need?
Usually one per product family or series, with model tables. Start with the families that matter most.
Our catalogue is in Chinese. Can you help?
Yes. We work from Chinese documents and write English pages with your team.
How long does it take?
It depends on the range. We usually start with a template and the top families, then add the rest in batches.
Will this improve our rankings?
It usually helps buyers and search find the right product, but nobody can guarantee rankings.
What about prices?
Most B2B product pages do not show prices; MOQs, lead times and an RFQ form work better.
